question.text: A wire of length <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>L</mi></math> and radius <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>r</mi></math> is clamped rigidly at one end. When the other end of the wire is pulled by a force<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mo> </mo><mi>f</mi></math>, its length increases by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>l</mi></math>. Another wire of same material of length <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>2</mn><mi>L</mi></math> and radius <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>2</mn><mi>r</mi></math> is pulled by a force <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>2</mn><mi>f</mi></math>. Then the increase in its length will be:

solution.text:
Young's modulus is same for both the wires since the material is same.

For the first wire,

Y=fLπr2l   ...(i)

For the second wire,

Y=2f(2L)4πr2l'   ...(ii)

Dividing (i) by (ii)

fLπr2l×4πr2l'4fL=1⇒l'=l
